exodus

EK-suh-dus — starts like 'exit'; an exodus is everyone exiting together, all at once. · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Exodus is a mass departure of a large number of people.

The approaching hurricane triggered a massive exodus of residents from the coastal towns.

Example

A factory that once employed most of a small town suddenly closes its doors for good. Within a year an exodus begins: hundreds of families pack up their belongings and move away, one after another, in search of new jobs elsewhere.

A huge number of people are leaving around the same time, for the same reason. Unlike 'trip,' which is usually about one person or a small group, exodus specifically describes a mass departure.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

migration: A migration is a relocation of people or animals to a new place to live, and the word looks toward where the travelers settle. An exodus stresses the departure itself, a place emptying out; it is always about the leaving, never the arriving.

evacuation: An evacuation is an organized removal of people from danger, usually ordered and directed by officials. An exodus needs no one in charge: it is simply a mass departure, and it can build family by family until a whole place stands empty.

emigration: Emigration is leaving your own country to settle permanently in another one. An exodus can happen at any scale of place, a town, a valley, an industry, and the word stresses the mass departure itself rather than the crossing of a border.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

arrival: the act of reaching or coming to a place

influx: a large number of people arriving somewhere

Where it sits · the scale and urgency of the leaving

departure → exodus → flight

departure vs. exodus: Departure is a plainer, weaker word than exodus — a departure can describe just one person leaving, while exodus specifically means a huge number of people leaving together.

flight vs. exodus: Flight can feel more urgent than exodus: an exodus can be planned or gradual, but flight suggests a hurried, often desperate escape from danger.

Build the Word

The pieces

Prefix — ex-: out (Greek)

Root — od: way, road, path (from Greek hodos; its h drops after ex- -- the same root in odometer)

Suffix — -us: the Latinized noun ending the word kept when it entered English

Put it together: Ex- ('out') + od ('way, road', from Greek hodos) + -us (the Latinized ending) spell exodus: 'the way out.' An exodus is, at its root, a large group finding the road out and leaving together.

Use the root in a new word: odometer: Dad tapped the odometer twice before backing out of the driveway.
